pi.name: Yujuan Su
pi.title: Assistant Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology
pi.bio: Yujuan Su holds a Ph.D. in neuroscience from the Chinese Academy of Sciences and completed postdoctoral training at UC San Diego, where she studied lung-innervating neurons and brainstem control of airway responses. She has received the Parker B. Francis Fellowship and an American Heart Association Career Development Award. She launched the Body-Brain Neural Circuits Lab in the Department of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology at the University of Michigan in July 2026.

description: The Su Lab (Body-Brain Neural Circuits Lab) studies body-brain communication in health and disease, using the lung-brain axis as a model for interoception. The lab asks how signals from the lung, including allergens, inflammation, toxins, and environmental exposures, are detected, transmitted through defined brainstem and higher brain pathways, and integrated in the central nervous system with cell-type specificity. It also investigates top-down neural circuits that regulate airway physiology and systemic responses, and how lung-brain circuits are remodeled in pulmonary and neurological disease. Approaches include neural circuit mapping, single-cell profiling, opto- and chemogenetics, electrophysiology, whole-animal physiology, and behavioral analysis, with the long-term goal of identifying targets for neuromodulation therapies.

areas.title: Lung-to-brain communication
areas.summary: How allergens, inflammation, toxins, and environmental exposures are sensed in the lung and relayed to the brain through defined brainstem and higher-order pathways with cell-type specificity.

areas.title: Central control of lung function
areas.summary: Top-down neural circuits that regulate airway physiology and systemic responses, with a focus on identifying molecular and functional specificity that could enable precise neuromodulation therapies.

areas.title: Circuit remodeling in disease
areas.summary: How lung-brain neural circuits become dysregulated in pulmonary and neurological diseases, and how perturbations reshape circuit activity and drive plasticity.

news.text: Jingyao Wang and Arovene Zheng joined as the lab's first rotation students.
The lab took its first group photo outside the museum.
Pranav Mudhas and Addy Szpiech joined as the lab's first undergraduate volunteers.

joining: The lab is recruiting postdoctoral researchers from a broad variety of backgrounds (neuroscience, physiology, immunology, body-brain interactions); apply by emailing a cover letter describing research interests and a CV with three references. Ph.D., M.D., and Master's students interested in the lab's interdisciplinary work should email to discuss rotation projects. There are currently no undergraduate openings, but applicants are encouraged to check back. Exchange scholars and summer researchers may reach out with a CV and summary of experience. The lab emphasizes mentorship tailored to individual career goals in a collaborative and supportive environment.
